analysis.one_liner: Requires social media platforms to protect minors from online harms and give parents supervision tools.
analysis.headline: Backed by senators from both parties and twice approved by the Senate Commerce Committee, the bill was placed on the Senate calendar but never came up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require apps and services likely used by people 16 or younger — social networks, messaging apps, video games, and streaming services — to act in a minor's best interest and take reasonable steps to prevent harms like promotion of suicide and eating disorders, addiction-like usage patterns, bullying, sexual exploitation, and ads for products illegal to sell to minors. Minors would get safety settings on by default (limits on who can contact them, opt-outs of algorithmic feeds, time limits, location restrictions), parents would get supervision tools, and large platforms would have to publish annual independent risk audits and let vetted researchers access data on harms. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rules. The bill never reached a Senate floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Minors under 17 and their parents gain enforceable rights against the platforms they use: best-interest obligations, safety defaults that cannot be steered away with manipulative design ('dark patterns'), parental supervision tools, a harm-reporting process with response deadlines, and annual public audits of how platforms' algorithms and design features may harm kids. Independent academic and nonprofit researchers also gain a legal channel to access platform data to study harms to minors. Parents of children 12 and under would get supervision tools enabled by default.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minors, their parents, and independent researchers

how_it_helps.text: Covered platforms must act in a minor's best interests and take reasonable measures in design and operation to prevent and mitigate harms including promotion of self-harm, suicide, eating disorders, addiction-like use patterns, bullying, sexual exploitation, and advertising of narcotics, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol to minors.

Minors get safeguards by default at the most protective level offered, including limits on who can contact or find them, restrictions on public access to their personal data and geolocation, controls on features that extend use such as autoplay and notifications, and the right to opt out of algorithmic recommendation systems that use their personal data.

Parents get tools to control privacy and account settings, restrict a minor's purchases and financial transactions, and track time spent on the platform, and for users the platform knows or reasonably believes to be a child (12 or younger) these tools are enabled by default.

The bill makes it unlawful to design a user interface with the purpose or substantial effect of subverting user choice in order to weaken or disable safeguards or parental controls, and requires an internal process to substantively respond to harm reports within 14 days.

Platforms averaging 10 million or more monthly U.S. users must publish annual public reports on risks to minors based on an independent third-party audit, disclose how their algorithms and targeted advertising use minors' personal data, and give approved academic and nonprofit researchers access to data assets for public-interest research on these harms.

The Federal Trade Commission enforces the Act as an unfair or deceptive practice, and state attorneys general may sue on behalf of their residents to enjoin violations and obtain damages or restitution.

analysis.who_pays: Large commercial platforms — social networks, messaging apps, video games, video streaming, and online services likely used by minors — bear the cost: redesigning defaults and feeds, building parental tools and reporting systems, running annual third-party audits, and accepting opt-outs and time limits that cut against engagement-driven advertising revenue. Platforms averaging fewer than 10 million U.S. users are exempt from the audit and researcher-access requirements. Taxpayers fund the FTC, Commerce, and NIST work through annual appropriations, and a device-level age verification system is studied but not mandated.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large social media, gaming, and streaming platforms

drawbacks.text: Parental tools let parents control a minor's privacy settings and are enabled by default for users a platform knows or reasonably believes to be a child; while the bill requires conspicuous notice to the minor when parental tools are in effect, the control sits with the parent, which civil liberties advocates warned could expose vulnerable teens — for example, those whose families are unsupportive — to monitoring or coerced account changes rather than protection.

The duty of care requires platforms to prevent and mitigate harms from 'materials on, or engagement with, the platform,' language broad enough that platforms could respond by aggressively filtering, restricting, or surveilling what teens can see and discuss rather than changing the design features the bill targets, and the reported version explicitly does not require platforms to collect any new age data or implement age gating, which limits how precisely they can even identify minors.

The burden falls heavily on large platforms: the audit and researcher-data requirements apply only to platforms averaging 10 million or more monthly U.S. users, and compliance, redesign, and audit costs are real even for well-resourced firms, with some of the cost likely passed into services used by everyone.

The bill only initiates a study of device-level age verification rather than resolving the hard question of how minors will be identified at all, so enforcement of the safeguards depends on platforms' existing age inference methods of uncertain accuracy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections respond to well-documented harms to young users, and the design is more careful than its critics allowed: the reported version requires 'reasonable measures' rather than strict liability, exempts small platforms, forbids new age-data collection mandates, and includes notice to minors when parents supervise them. The honest objections are that the duty-of-care language could invite over-broad content restrictions on teens, and that handing parents default control over a teen's privacy settings can cut both ways — protection for some kids, surveillance for others. On balance, the bill would have shifted real power over minors' online experience from advertising-driven platform design to families and regulators, at meaningful but manageable cost to large platforms.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved it twice and it was placed on the Senate's calendar of pending business in December 2022, but the Senate never took it up before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the bill on February 16, 2022 with a bipartisan group of 13 original cosponsors led by Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.

On July 27, 2022 the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and on December 15, 2022 Chairwoman Maria Cantwell formally reported it to the Senate with that substitute amendment.

The reported version softened some provisions of the introduced bill, for example requiring 'reasonable measures' under the duty of care and exempting platforms averaging fewer than 10 million monthly U.S. users from the audit and researcher-access requirements.

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 660 on December 15, 2022, where it remained with no floor debate or vote recorded before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large social media and gaming platforms came out ahead: the bill died after clearing committee and landing on the Senate calendar, so none of the duty-of-care obligations, default safeguards, parental tools, annual independent audits, algorithmic opt-outs, or researcher data-access requirements ever took effect, leaving platforms' engagement-driven design and ad targeting of young users unchanged. Families and researchers gained nothing from this version.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large social media and gaming platforms

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Kids Online Safety Act and assembled a bipartisan group of original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction as the lead Republican, lending it bipartisan cover.

for.name: Maria Cantwell
for.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill through committee — ordered reported favorably in July 2022 and formally reported it to the Senate with a substitute amendment on December 15, 2022.

for.name: 7 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (7 of the 13 cosponsors were Republicans).

for.name: 6 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (6 of the 13 cosponsors were Democrats).

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote after it was reported and placed on the legislative calendar; the record shows no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: NetChoice
against.role: Trade association for major online platforms including Meta, Google, and TikTok
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the duty-of-care and parental-oversight provisions as vague, burdensome, and a threat to free expression online, opposing the bill and its later versions.

against.name: Civil liberties and LGBTQ youth advocacy groups
against.what_they_did: Argued that default parental surveillance and broad platform filtering duties could censor what vulnerable teens, including LGBTQ youth, could access and could push them off safer platforms.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with a Republican lead cosponsor, and its 13 cosponsors split 7 Republicans and 6 Democrats; no vote was ever taken, so the parties' full positions were never recorded.

industries.industry: Social media, messaging, gaming, and video streaming platforms
industries.note: The bill imposes a duty of care to minors, protective defaults, parental tools, dark-pattern prohibitions, annual independent audits, and algorithmic opt-outs on platforms likely used by minors, and their ad-supported business models depend on the engagement and data collection those rules curtail. Their interest in killing or narrowing the bill ran directly against the bill's purpose for families.

Platforms would have to disclose how minors' personal data is used to target ads, give minors and parents ways to limit or opt out of algorithmic recommendations, and stop advertising products illegal to sell to minors, cutting off part of the youth-targeted ad market and its data pipeline.

The bill creates a program giving approved university and 501(c)(3) researchers access to platform data assets to study harms to minors, plus a safe harbor for data collection in such research, ending platforms' ability to keep that data sealed. The same access directly serves the public's interest in knowing what the platforms do to kids.

industries.industry: Small online platforms (under 10 million U.S. users)
industries.note: The reported bill exempts platforms averaging fewer than 10 million monthly U.S. users from the annual audit and researcher data-access requirements, shielding startups and niche services from most compliance costs. The exemption is a competitive carve-out, though the duty of care and safeguards still apply to them.
